summary: A news story dated October 11, 2023 describes a week of tremors and earthquakes in the Tokyo area, including a magnitude 6.7 quake on October 4th that damaged coastal infrastructure and closed airports. It covers the emergency response, infrastructure vulnerabilities, Tokyo's tectonic setting, community preparedness, economic costs, early warning upgrades, international cooperation and calls for more resilience funding.
one_line: Following a magnitude 6.7 earthquake on October 4, 2023, Tokyo reviews disaster preparedness, infrastructure risks, early warning upgrades and resilience funding.
key_facts: On September 23rd, a magnitude 4.5 earthquake struck the Izu Peninsula south of Tokyo; Dr. Hirotaka Nakamura called it a bellwether of stress accumulation along faultlines near Tokyo.
On October 4th, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake damaged infrastructure and residential areas, primarily along coastal regions.
The October 4th quake hit during rush hour at Tokyo Bay's core, disrupting transport, causing widespread blackouts and temporarily closing Narita and Haneda airports.
Governor Yuriko Koike led first responders in assessing and addressing immediate damage after the quake.
Urban planner Kenji Watanabe and his team of engineers are assessing buildings, bridges and public transportation systems for retrofitting.
Tokyo sits at the junction of four tectonic plates: Pacific, North American, Eurasian and Philippine Sea.
Mika Yoshida leads regular drills and educational programs at community centers and works with local schools to integrate disaster readiness into curricula.
Yasuo Takahashi, head of Tokyo Chamber of Commerce, reported supply chain and financial market disruptions, saying every minute of downtime can lead to millions in losses.

The Japan Meteorological Agency's early warning system uses sensors detecting P-waves to give warning before damaging S-waves arrive; upgrades to improve accuracy and lead times have been prioritized.
Delegations from countries such as Chile and New Zealand came to Tokyo to share earthquake expertise.

Seiji Maehara, Minister of Infrastructure and Transport, advocates increased budgets and a nationwide review of seismic preparedness, saying "Investing in resilience not only saves lives but also makes economic sense in the long run."
The article references the 2011 Great East Japan earthquake as a still-fresh collective memory.
